stem: An 8-year-old boy with asthma has had attacks every month over winter, was discharged from PICU a few days ago after a severe attack, wakes at night at least 5 days every week, wheezes with exercise, and uses salbutamol at least once a day. When well, what preventer and dose would you write in the Asthma Action Plan?

options.text: Flixotide junior (50mcg) MDI 2 puffs twice per day
Seretide 50/25 mcg MDI 2 puffs twice per day
Seretide 125/25 mcg MDI 2 puffs twice per day

explanation: This child has very poorly controlled, severe persistent asthma with frequent symptoms, nocturnal waking, exercise limitation, daily reliever use, and a recent PICU admission. A high-dose inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting beta2-agonist preventer is appropriate; among the options, Seretide 125/25 mcg 2 puffs twice daily is the best choice.
rationale: The question asks for the preventer to write when the child is well. His symptoms and recent PICU admission indicate severe persistent asthma requiring a step-up to combination therapy at higher dose.

optionExplanations.A: Inappropriate because he clearly needs controller therapy.
optionExplanations.B: Montelukast alone is insufficient for this degree of asthma severity.
optionExplanations.C: Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid alone is too weak for severe uncontrolled asthma.
optionExplanations.D: Same as C; the dose is too low for this presentation.
optionExplanations.E: This combination is lower strength than the more appropriate high-dose option.
optionExplanations.F: Same as E; wording varies but dose remains low.
optionExplanations.G: Best option: high-dose ICS/LABA preventer for severe poorly controlled asthma.
optionExplanations.H: Same medication as G but ambiguous wording; G is the standard concise dosing format.
